title: Four Square Mile Wells: Depth, Yield and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Four Square Mile well records show a 27 ft median depth, but monitoring wells dominate. Compare yields, drilling costs and buyer checks.
h1: Understanding wells around Four Square Mile
intro_html:
A shallow well record near Four Square Mile does not necessarily tell you what a household water supply will require. Monitoring accounts for 66% of permitted uses in this dataset, while domestic and household use accounts for 11%. That distinction matters before you use the local depth median to budget a new well.

These figures cover permitted wells within 5 miles of Four Square Mile, not just wells inside the neighborhood. They provide useful context around Holly Hills, Glendale and Cherry Hills Village, but the right comparison is a nearby well with the same purpose and aquifer as your proposed supply.

sections.heading: Why the 27-foot median needs context here
sections.html:
Among the 4,021 records reporting depth, the median is 27 feet and the middle half runs 20–50 feet. Wells under 100 feet account for 87% of the depth mix. Those figures describe a predominantly shallow record set, not a dependable target depth for a new household well.

The deeper end is substantial: the 90th percentile is 250 feet, and the deepest recorded well reaches 2,265 feet. Permits name Alluvial and Denver aquifers, while many leave the aquifer unnamed or use a fractured-bedrock category. Ask a driller to identify the intended water-bearing formation and suitable nearby supply wells. A bid based only on the neighborhood median could describe the wrong kind of hole.

sections.heading: Reported yield is not a household supply guarantee
sections.html:
Only 148 wells report a pump yield, compared with 7,062 total permit records. Their median is 15.0 gpm, with a middle half of 10.0–99.0 gpm. That broad spread, combined with the mix of well uses, makes the median a reference point rather than a promise for your lot.

At the low end, 4% report under 1 gpm and 9% fall in the 1–5 gpm band. A buyer considering a low-yield well should budget for evaluation of recovery, storage and household demand before closing. Obtain the actual pumping-test information and confirm what the permit authorizes. A reported pumping rate does not establish sustainable production or permission to irrigate a yard.

sections.heading: Shallow water levels do not show a falling table
sections.html:
The 153 records with static water levels have a median depth to water of 14 feet below ground; the middle half is 11–19 feet. Static level measures where water stands in an idle well. It is not the total drilled depth, and it does not tell you how far the level drops while pumping.

Decade medians change from 16 feet in the 2010s to 14 feet in the 2020s. That does not show a dropping water table: the later median is shallower. It also does not prove aquifer recovery, because these summaries may represent different wells and aquifers. For a purchase, repeated measurements from the subject well are more useful than this area-wide comparison.

sections.heading: A permit history dominated by monitoring work
sections.html:
Permit issuance was highest in the supplied decade totals during the 2000s, with 1,840 permits, following 1,809 in the 1990s. The records show 902 in the 2010s and 477 in the 2020s, with the newest permit dated 2025. The latest decade is incomplete, so avoid treating that comparison as a direct measure of declining activity.

Of 7,062 permits, 3,248 are recorded as constructed. The most frequent listed driller entry is “Authorized (Pe, Pg)” at 2,939; that is not a conventional company name. Ground Exploration Llc (Bender, Joseph T.) appears on 291 records and Hier Drilling Co Inc (Hier, Bruce A.) on 103. Given the monitoring-heavy use mix, record frequency alone does not establish household-well experience or current availability.

sections.heading: What the shallow-depth cost model actually buys
sections.html:
The supplied model uses Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock and a drilling rate of $50–$70 per foot. At the 27-foot median depth, it estimates about $1,400–$1,900 for the drilled hole and $7,400–$13,900 for a finished well with pump, tank, trenching and electrical.

Treat that as a shallow-depth illustration, not a household-well quote for Four Square Mile. The monitoring-heavy records can make the median a poor match for a domestic supply. Ask for a written scope tied to the permitted aquifer and proposed depth, with casing, grout, pump selection, testing and site access clearly addressed. Also ask how the contractor handles additional depth or an unsuccessful hole before authorizing work.

sections.heading: Environmental checks matter around Four Square Mile
sections.html:
Within about 10 miles, the mapped inventory includes 631 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 170 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. These are screening flags, not proof that a particular well is contaminated. A PFAS sampling location does not necessarily mean contamination was detected, and nearby cleanup activity does not establish a connection to your aquifer.

Review site details and have a qualified laboratory test the subject well for drinking-water suitability, including contaminants indicated by local conditions. Inspect the cap, casing and surface drainage as well. Where septic is proposed, confirm local approval, setbacks and soil suitability before fixing the house location. Low yield and an unsuccessful bore remain separate risks that environmental screening cannot resolve.

sections.heading: Before buying a lot near Holly Hills or Glendale
sections.html:
Start with the parcel's actual water-service options and Colorado DWR permit status, not the nearest dot on the map. Around Four Square Mile, Holly Hills and Glendale, a nearby monitoring well is not evidence that your parcel can obtain a household well. Confirm the allowed uses, aquifer and whether the existing permit matches the constructed well.

For an existing supply, request the completion report, pumping information, water-quality results and maintenance history. For a build, compare neighboring domestic wells and get a site-specific drilling proposal before finalizing the budget. Coordinate rig access, driveway grading, utility trenches and any septic area with the building plan. Resolve water availability and authorization before committing to a layout that depends on them.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Four Square Mile, Colorado?
faq.a: Within 5 miles of Four Square Mile, reported well depths have a 27-foot median and a middle half of 20–50 feet. However, monitoring accounts for 66% of permitted uses, so these shallow figures are not a reliable household-well target. Compare nearby domestic wells in the intended aquifer before accepting a proposed drilling depth.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Four Square Mile?
faq.a: The supplied model uses $50–$70 per foot. At the area's 27-foot median depth, the drilled hole is about $1,400–$1,900, and a finished well with pump, tank, trenching and electrical is about $7,400–$13,900. Because monitoring wells dominate the records, a domestic well may require a different depth and scope. Get a parcel-specific quote.

faq.q: How much water do wells produce in Four Square Mile?
faq.a: The 148 records reporting pump yield have a median of 15.0 gpm and a middle half of 10.0–99.0 gpm. At the low end, 4% report under 1 gpm. Those figures cover mixed well uses, not just homes. Have the subject well's sustained production and recovery evaluated rather than relying on the area median.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Four Square Mile?
faq.a: The supplied records cannot establish whether an individual well is safe. The nearby environmental inventory includes 631 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 170 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites within about 10 miles. Those counts warrant investigation, not an assumption of contamination. Review relevant site records and obtain laboratory testing from the well you intend to use.

faq.q: Is the water table dropping in Four Square Mile?
faq.a: The available decade medians do not show a decline: depth to water was 16 feet in the 2010s and 14 feet in the 2020s, meaning the later median was shallower. However, only 153 records report static levels, and the decades may include different wells. Repeated measurements from the same well are needed to assess its trend.
